solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Be near opening of sheep fold

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, so only the start of the next word is kept

parts.note: the first letter of sheep
to crimp is to press into small folds or pleats

explanation.surface: Someone is told to stand close to the entrance of a sheep pen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fold' looks like a sheep enclosure to match the scene, but here it is a crease. 'Near' is the old sense of stingy.
explanation.definitionFit: Near can mean mean or tight with money, so being near is to economise stingily, to scrimp.

clue.text: Greek character taps letters on one

parts.note: taps are marked C for cold and H for hot
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A Greek person taps out letters on a keyboard or typewriter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' reads as a person from Greece; it is a letter of the Greek alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Chi is the twenty-second letter of the Greek alphabet, written like an X.

clue.text: Completely reversed

definitions.meaning: first meaning: thoroughly, as when you know something this way
second meaning: turned so the lining faces outwards

explanation.walkthrough: The two words look like one phrase about total reversal, but each is a separate meaning of the same expression.
explanation.definitionFit: Knowing a subject inside out means knowing it thoroughly, and a garment turned inside out has its inner side showing.

clue.text: Flap wings in agitation, captured by photo

indicators.note: something captured is held inside its captor, so these letters go within the other piece

parts.note: pic is short for picture or photo

indicators.note: the wings of a word are its two outer letters, left and right like a bird's

parts.note: the first and last letters of agitation

explanation.surface: A bird flaps its wings in alarm and is caught on camera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flap' looks like the start of the bird picture but is the definition, and 'wings' is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a flap is informal for being in a state of anxious alarm, the same as panic.

clue.text: Official makes you see old lady during bath time

indicators.note: something happening during a period falls within it, so these letters sit inside the other pieces

parts.note: a dip is a quick bathe
lo is an old word meaning look or see
ma is an informal word for mother, the old lady
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: An official arranges for you to visit an elderly woman at her bathtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old lady' is slang for mother, not a pensioner, and 'you see' is the old exclamation lo.
explanation.definitionFit: A diplomat is an official representing their country abroad in dealings with foreign governments.

clue.text: Partners enthralled by god's body

indicators.note: someone enthralled is held captive, so these letters are held within the other word

parts.note: a deity is a god; the apostrophe-s reads as 'god is', a link
North and South are partners in the card game bridge

explanation.surface: A couple are captivated by the physique of a deity.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridge is played in partnerships named after compass points, North-South against East-West.
explanation.definitionFit: Body can mean thickness or consistency, as in a wine or sauce with body, which is a matter of density.

clue.text: Keep going over each training period?

definitions.note: the question mark flags that this is one example of such a period

indicators.note: one thing placed over another covers it, so this phrase wraps around the next piece

parts.note: to press on is to continue despite difficulty
ea is the standard abbreviation for each

explanation.surface: An instruction to persevere through every training session.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for keep going is split by the abbreviation, which lands after its fourth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Sports teams spend the weeks before competition starts getting fit, so the preseason is a time of training.

clue.text: Neat border plant

parts.note: neat is an old word for cattle, and an ox is one
a lip is the rim or edge of something

explanation.surface: A tidy edging plant in a garden bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' looks like tidy, but it is the archaic word for cattle, still seen in neatsfoot oil.
explanation.definitionFit: The oxlip is a wild flower of the primrose family, related to the cowslip.

clue.text: On account of mouth filling, swallowed ice

parts.note: as means because or on account of
mouth and sass both mean cheeky backchat
a filling is inside something
to swallow food is to eat it

explanation.surface: Someone swallowed ice because a mouth filling was hurting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mouth filling' suggests dentistry; it splits into two pieces. Ice is underworld slang for kill.
explanation.definitionFit: In American gangster slang to ice someone is to kill them, and assassinate means to murder a prominent target.

clue.text: Tingling in legs, also hands

parts.note: pins is informal for legs
and means also or in addition
the hands of a dial or gauge are its needles

explanation.surface: A prickly sensation is felt in the legs and the hands too.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a single medical complaint; 'in' is only the link.
explanation.definitionFit: Pins and needles is the everyday name for the prickly sensation when a numb limb wakes up.

clue.text: For Channel 4, English is valuable

parts.note: pro means in favour of, for
a duct is a channel or tube
IV is the Roman numeral for four
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A remark that English programming is valuable for the TV station Channel 4.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Channel 4' is a British TV network, but here the two words are read separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Productive work yields useful results, so it is valuable in the sense of being worthwhile.

clue.text: Commanding respect, waves to Bluebeard

indicators.note: waves are in constant motion, so these letters are tossed into a new order

parts.note: the eleven letters used as written

explanation.surface: A feared figure waves a greeting to the fairy-tale wife-killer Bluebeard.
explanation.walkthrough: Bluebeard is the murderous husband of the French folk tale; he supplies letters only.
explanation.definitionFit: A redoubtable person is formidable, inspiring awe and respect because of their strength or ability.

clue.text: Dad's meeting son while away

parts.note: pa is dad, plus the S of the possessive
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A father meets up with his son while the son is away from home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'While' looks like a conjunction meaning during; with 'away' it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To while away time is to spend it idly, and passing the time means exactly that.

clue.text: You'd soil pants in a horrible way

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish or badly done, so these letters are poorly arranged

parts.note: the letters used as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A toilet joke: you would mess your trousers in a horrible way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' reads as underwear or trousers to soil, but it is the slang adjective for poor.
explanation.definitionFit: Odious means hateful or repugnant, so acting odiously is behaving in a horrible manner.

clue.text: Homes were demolished in unknown location

indicators.note: demolished buildings are knocked down and their parts left jumbled, so these letters are rebuilt differently

parts.note: the nine letters used as written

explanation.surface: Houses were knocked down at a spot nobody can identify.
explanation.definitionFit: Somewhere refers to a place that is not named or specified, an unidentified spot.

clue.text: Room designer may get one over on boss

indicators.note: in an across entry, one thing on another is placed after it, so these letters follow the next piece

parts.note: a boss is a raised knob or stud on a surface
the Roman numeral for one
O is the cricket scoresheet abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: An interior designer hopes to get the better of their employer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get one over on boss' suggests outwitting a manager; read 'on' as 'placed after', so I and O follow STUD.
explanation.definitionFit: A studio is a workroom where a designer or artist works, so it is a room a designer may get.

clue.text: Put out after doing OK

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming after means placed below, so this piece follows the next one

parts.note: what are you up to means what are you doing
to snuff a candle is to put it out

explanation.surface: Someone is annoyed after being told they did all right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' looks like 'annoyed'; it is extinguish.
explanation.definitionFit: Something up to snuff meets the required standard, adequate and acceptable.

clue.text: Trade convention

definitions.meaning: first meaning: business from regular buyers, patronage
second meaning: a habitual practice or tradition

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a trade fair or conference; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop's regular patronage is its custom, and an established practice or tradition is also a custom.

clue.text: Rat skirting a trap set by old pest controller

indicators.note: to skirt something is to go round its edge, so this word wraps around the rest

parts.note: a rat and a cad are both scoundrels
taken as written
a net is a trap
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A rat dodges a trap laid by a veteran exterminator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rat' sounds like the pest in the scene; it is the scoundrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Cane toads were introduced to Australia to eat beetles in sugar fields, making them a would-be biological pest control, though they became pests themselves.

clue.text: Bluff — a need for binding agreement

parts.note: to bluff someone is to con them
cord or string is needed to tie something up

explanation.surface: A deceptive tactic is needed to secure a binding contract.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Binding agreement' looks like a single legal phrase; binding belongs with the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Concord means harmony between people or a formal treaty, both senses of agreement.

clue.text: Go mad on retirement

indicators.note: retiring is withdrawing or going back, so the word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: bats is slang for crazy

explanation.surface: A warning that people go crazy once they stop working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go mad' looks like one phrase; 'Go' alone is the definition, as in 'have a go'.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a go and having a stab are both idioms for making an attempt.

clue.text: Go off right, opening chest

indicators.note: something opening a body pushes into it, so this letter is put inside the other word

parts.note: the bust is the chest
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A gun goes off, the bullet striking the right side and opening the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: A bomb or balloon that goes off explodes, and to burst is to break apart suddenly.

clue.text: Wine out of case, ultimately for bottle

indicators.note: here 'out of' means on the outside of, so this word wraps around the following one

parts.note: taken as written
a chest is a box or case

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the last letter of for

explanation.surface: Wine taken from its case, eventually poured into a bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of' looks like 'taken from'; it means on the outside of, so the drink wraps the box.
explanation.definitionFit: A winchester is a large glass bottle, traditionally holding about half a gallon, used for chemicals.

clue.text: A male auction item?

parts.note: he is the pronoun for a male
each item put up at auction is a lot

explanation.surface: A man being sold off at an auction.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a whole, the clue describes a man who could be sold as property; the question mark admits it is a description by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A helot was a serf of ancient Sparta, owned like property; the term extends to any slave.

clue.text: The butt of many a joke?

definitions.text: The butt of many a joke?

parts.words: The butt of many a joke?
parts.note: surface reading: the person everyone makes fun of
setter's reading: a butt is a large cask, here one holding a great many jokes, so a very funny person

explanation.walkthrough: A butt is both a target of ridicule and a large wine cask; the cask holding many laughs describes a hilarious person.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrel of laughs is an idiom for someone or something extremely entertaining and fun.

clue.text: Fly that is chasing husband

indicators.note: one who chases runs behind, so this piece comes after the other

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for husband
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: An insect is pursuing a married man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' looks like the insect; it is the verb meaning hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: Hie is an old word meaning to go quickly or hasten, as one does when flying off.

clue.text: I have some cows and three horses around?

indicators.note: horsing around is messing about, so these letters are played with until they rearrange

parts.note: the eight letters used as written

explanation.surface: A farmer boasts of owning a few cattle and three horses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horses' looks like animals on the farm, but 'horses around' is the instruction. Neat is an old word for cattle.
explanation.definitionFit: A neatherd is a cowherd, someone who tends cattle, so he could say he has cows in his charge.

clue.text: Sweet result of feeding sandwiches

indicators.note: a sandwich holds its filling between outer slices, so the wanted letters lie enclosed within these words

parts.note: the letters run across the three words, from the last of result to the middle of feeding

explanation.surface: A sweet treat is the outcome of eating sandwiches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' looks like food in the eating scene, but it is the verb meaning holds inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Toffee is a chewy confection made by boiling sugar and butter, a classic British sweet.
